steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on regularization for blind image super-resolution: we argue Dropout is a poor choice and propose aligning feature statistics across differently degraded copies of the same image instead. Include a contributions list.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
With the explosive advancement of deep learning technology, Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) with deep neural networks (DNNs) has developed a lot in recent years (e.g., VDSR, SRResNet, EDSR, RDN and SwinIR), and these models perform better than traditional prediction models.

But collecting a massive amount of natural low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) image pairs to train DNNs is a non-trivial issue, so early SISR researchers used manually designed HR/LR image pairs (i.e., bicubic) instead. However, realistic degradations hardly follow such a simple assumption, and this leads to a severe performance drop for these models.

Blind SR is an answer to this question, and it tries to improve the model generalization ability with unknown degradations. Promising results have been obtained by enriching the training degradation space (e.g., through handcrafted synthesisation or data distribution learning) and by enhancing the model capability (e.g., unfolding the degradation model or exploring image internal statistics). But we notice that training strategy (regularization) that helps Blind SR has barely been investigated so far.

In this paper, we argue that this investigation is necessary and meaningful given the current research status of Blind SR, for the following reasons. First, without enlarging the degradation space for training, the development of Blind SR has reached its bottleneck. There are methods that try to excavate the internal similar patterns of an image to do zero-shot learning, but they can easily fail in natural cases where there are no self-repeated patterns. On the other hand, training with a large degradation space in theory gives the model better generalization ability, because it encourages the model to focus more on learning the shape and texture prior of natural images. So constructing a diverse degradation pool for training (called data-driven based Blind SR, according to prior work) has become a mainstream direction for recent Blind SR research, and it has been shown to be effective in CNN-based, GAN-based and Diffusion-based models.

- Overfitting to degradation; Dropout
  - only ideally does diverse training learn degradation invariant representation and generalize
  - other fields warn: without regularization, not easily achieved
  - prior work first noticed; refreshed Dropout against "overfitting to degradation"; scaling data/network alone no longer improves generalization
  - but Dropout side-effects: less feature interaction and diversity -> loss of vivid high frequency details; Fig. 1; analysis in Sec. 3
- Our method
  - problem comes from excessive attention on specific degradations
  - statistical alignment: align first/second order feature statistics (mean, covariance) of two images, same content, different degradations
  - model removes degradation-related info in forward pass -> recovers fine-grained HR content, more generalizable
  - model-agnostic; pre-request (same content, different degradations) fits data-driven Blind SR with stochastic degradation-generation models
  - details in Sec. 4
- Contributions
  - Dropout not desirable for Blind SR: reduces feature interaction/diversity, loses high frequency details (theory + experiments)
  - simple statistical alignment -> model unaware of degradation; parallel/complementary to data-driven Blind SR
  - experiments on seven widely used benchmarks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
With the explosive advancement of deep learning technology, Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) with deep neural networks (DNNs) has developed a lot in recent years (e.g., VDSR, SRResNet, EDSR, RDN and SwinIR), and these models perform better than traditional prediction models.

But collecting a massive amount of natural low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) image pairs to train DNNs is a non-trivial issue, so early SISR researchers used manually designed HR/LR image pairs (i.e., bicubic) instead. However, realistic degradations hardly follow such a simple assumption, and this leads to a severe performance drop for these models.

Blind SR is an answer to this question, and it tries to improve the model generalization ability with unknown degradations. Promising results have been obtained by enriching the training degradation space (e.g., through handcrafted synthesisation or data distribution learning) and by enhancing the model capability (e.g., unfolding the degradation model or exploring image internal statistics). But we notice that training strategy (regularization) that helps Blind SR has barely been investigated so far.

In this paper, we argue that this investigation is necessary and meaningful given the current research status of Blind SR, for the following reasons. First, without enlarging the degradation space for training, the development of Blind SR has reached its bottleneck. There are methods that try to excavate the internal similar patterns of an image to do zero-shot learning, but they can easily fail in natural cases where there are no self-repeated patterns. On the other hand, training with a large degradation space in theory gives the model better generalization ability, because it encourages the model to focus more on learning the shape and texture prior of natural images. So constructing a diverse degradation pool for training (called data-driven based Blind SR, according to prior work) has become a mainstream direction for recent Blind SR research, and it has been shown to be effective in CNN-based, GAN-based and Diffusion-based models.

However, only in ideal circumstances can the model trained with diverse degradations automatically unleash its full potential to learn a degradation invariant representation and so become more generalizable to unknown degradations. Experiences from other fields warn that without proper regularization this ideal case may not be easy to achieve. Recently, one work first noticed this problem and refreshed the use of Dropout to mitigate the "overfitting to degradation" issue in data-driven Blind SR. They pointed out that without proper regularization, simply increasing the data and network scale can not keep improving the generalization ability anymore. But we notice that even though performance improves, Dropout also introduces unwanted side-effects that reduce feature interaction and diversity, and this leads to the loss of vivid high frequency details. We show a preliminary example in Fig. 1, and the theoretical and experimental analyses are in Sec. 3.

Also, the "overfitting to degradation" problem comes from the network paying excessive attention to some specific degradations. To deal with this, we propose a statistical alignment method that, during training, aligns the first and second order feature statistics (i.e., mean and covariance) of two images that have the same content but different degradations. We observe that this simple regularization effectively improves the model's ability to selectively remove degradation-related information during the forward pass. So the model can recover fine-grained HR contents without being distracted by degradations, and it becomes more generalizable. Our regularization can easily work with existing popular DNNs in a model-agnostic way, and its implementation pre-request (i.e., images with the same content but different degradations) works smoothly with current data-driven Blind SR methods that have stochastic degradation-generation models. The details of our method are in Sec. 4, and here we summarize the main contributions of this paper:

- We argue and verify both theoretically and experimentally that Dropout is not a good regularization choice for the Blind SR setting, because of its side-effect of reducing feature interaction and diversity, which leads to losing information, especially in high frequency details.

- We propose a simple statistical alignment method that encourages the model to be completely unaware of degradation information, so the full potential of model generalization ability is excavated. Our regularization works in parallel with and is a complement to existing data-driven Blind SR research.

- We do extensive experiments on seven widely used benchmarks to validate our proposals and arguments.

steps.text:

Nevertheless, realistic degradations barely obey such a simple assumption, leading to a severe performance drop for these models.

Blind SR [12,13,14,15,16], as an answer to this problem, seeks to improve model generalization ability with unknown degradations. In this paper, we argue that such an investigation is necessary and meaningful, given the current research status of Blind SR, for the following reasons. Firstly, without enlarging the degradation space for training, the development of Blind SR has reached its bottleneck [12,19]. Even though there are methods trying to excavate an image's internal similar patterns to perform zero-shot learning [24,23], they can easily fail in natural cases where self-repeated patterns are absent. On the other hand, training with a large degradation space theoretically grants the model better generalization ability by encouraging it to focus more on learning the shape and texture prior of natural images. - We argue and verify both theoretically and experimentally that Dropout is not a desirable regularization choice for the Blind SR setting due to its side-effect of reducing feature interaction and diversity, which further leads to losing information, especially in high frequency details.

Note that our regularization works in parallel with, and serves as a complement to, existing data-driven Blind SR research.
